theory.overview: Gradient Descent is the engine that powers neural network training. It's an optimization algorithm that minimizes the loss function by iteratively moving in the direction of steepest decrease. Imagine standing on a mountain in thick fog—you feel the slope under your feet and take a step downhill. Repeat until you reach the valley (minimum loss). This simple yet powerful idea, combined with backpropagation for computing gradients, enables neural networks to learn from data by adjusting billions of parameters.

sections.title: The Core Idea
sections.content: At its heart, gradient descent is calculus in action. The gradient points in the direction of greatest increase, so we move in the opposite direction. The learning rate controls step size—too small and learning is slow, too large and we might overshoot the minimum.
sections.intuition: Subtract the gradient (scaled by learning rate) from current weights to reduce loss

sections.title: Types of Gradient Descent
sections.content: The choice of how many samples to use for each gradient calculation creates a spectrum from precise but slow to fast but noisy.

types.name: Batch Gradient Descent
types.description: Use ALL training data for each update

types.name: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
types.description: Use ONE random sample per update

types.name: Mini-batch Gradient Descent
types.bestPractice: This is the standard choice in deep learning

sections.title: Learning Rate: The Critical Hyperparameter
sections.content: The learning rate is arguably the most important hyperparameter. Too high: loss explodes or oscillates. Too low: training takes forever or gets stuck in poor local minima.

schedules.name: Step Decay
schedules.description: Drop learning rate every s epochs

schedules.name: ReduceLROnPlateau
schedules.description: Drop LR when validation loss plateaus

sections.title: Challenges in Optimization
sections.content: The loss landscape of deep neural networks is complex—full of local minima, saddle points, and flat regions. Understanding these challenges helps diagnose training issues.

challenges.name: Local Minima
challenges.description: Points where gradient is zero but not the global minimum
challenges.reality: In high dimensions, local minima are rare; saddle points dominate

challenges.name: Saddle Points
challenges.description: Points where gradient is zero but it's a minimum in some directions, maximum in others
challenges.problem: Gradient descent can get stuck or slow down significantly

challenges.name: Ill-Conditioning
challenges.description: Loss curves are much steeper in some directions than others
challenges.symptom: Slow progress in flat directions, instability in steep directions

challenges.name: Plateaus
challenges.description: Flat regions where gradients are near zero

sections.title: Momentum and Acceleration
sections.content: Momentum adds 'velocity' to parameter updates, accumulating gradients over time. This helps in consistent directions and dampens oscillations—like a ball rolling down a hill gaining speed.

nesterov.description: Look ahead to where momentum will take us, then compute gradient

keyConcepts.name: Loss Landscape
keyConcepts.description: The high-dimensional surface defined by the loss function over all possible parameter values.
keyConcepts.analogy: Like a mountain range where valleys are minima and peaks are maxima

keyConcepts.name: Convergence
keyConcepts.description: Reaching a point where loss stops decreasing significantly (ideally at a minimum).
keyConcepts.criteria: Loss changes < threshold for N consecutive epochs

keyConcepts.name: Epoch vs Iteration
keyConcepts.description: An epoch is one full pass through all training data. An iteration is one parameter update (one batch).

keyConcepts.name: Stochasticity
keyConcepts.description: Randomness in SGD from sampling batches. Helps escape sharp minima and can improve generalization.

complexity.perEpoch: $O(N \cdot n\_params)$ where N = training set size
complexity.note: Most computation is in forward/backward passes, not the update itself

steps.title: Initialize Parameters
steps.description: Start with random weights (typically small values) and set learning rate.

steps.title: Compute Gradient
steps.description: Calculate the slope of the loss function at current position.

steps.title: Update Parameters
steps.description: Move in the opposite direction of the gradient (downhill).

steps.title: Repeat Until Convergence
steps.description: Continue until gradient is near zero or max iterations reached.

steps.title: Add Momentum
steps.description: With momentum, we accumulate velocity for faster convergence.

practiceProblems.title: Simple Gradient Descent
practiceProblems.description: For $L(w) = w^2$, start at $w_0 = 3$, learning rate $\eta = 0.2$. Compute $w_1$ and $w_2$.

practiceProblems.title: Learning Rate Impact
practiceProblems.description: For $L(w) = w^2$ starting at $w = 5$, compare convergence with $\eta = 0.1$, $\eta = 0.5$, $\eta = 1.1$.
practiceProblems.answer: $\eta = 0.1$: converges slowly | $\eta = 0.5$: converges optimally | $\eta = 1.1$: DIVERGES (oscillates outward)
practiceProblems.explanation: With $\eta > 1$, we overshoot: $w_1 = 5 - 1.1(10) = -6$, then $w_2 = -6 - 1.1(-12) = 7.2$, growing larger each step!

practiceProblems.title: Batch Size Trade-offs
practiceProblems.description: For a dataset of 10,000 examples, compare batch sizes 1 (SGD), 100, and 10,000 (batch GD).
practiceProblems.answer: SGD: 10,000 noisy updates per epoch, fast iteration, escapes minima | Batch 100: 100 smoother updates, vectorized, good balance | Batch 10,000: 1 precise update, slow, may get stuck
practiceProblems.explanation: Small batches provide noise (regularization) and frequent updates but high variance. Large batches have lower variance but less exploration. Mini-batch (32-512) is the sweet spot for GPU efficiency.

practiceProblems.title: Saddle Point Escape
practiceProblems.description: At a saddle point, gradient is zero in all directions. How does gradient descent escape?
practiceProblems.answer: Pure GD gets stuck! But SGD's noise from random sampling provides perturbations that can push off the saddle. Momentum also helps by continuing motion from previous steps.
practiceProblems.explanation: In high dimensions, saddle points are much more common than local minima. SGD's stochasticity is actually a feature here—it naturally escapes saddles. This is one reason SGD often outperforms batch GD in deep learning.
hints: Exact zero gradient means no update
Momentum carries you through flat regions

practiceProblems.title: Learning Rate Schedule
practiceProblems.description: Design a learning rate schedule for training a ResNet on ImageNet for 90 epochs.
practiceProblems.answer: Warmup: epochs 1-5, linearly increase from 0 to 0.1 | Main training: epochs 6-30 at 0.1 | Decay: drop to 0.01 at epoch 30, 0.001 at epoch 60 | Cosine annealing alternative: smooth decay from 0.1 to 0 following cosine curve
practiceProblems.explanation: Warmup prevents early instability. Step decay is simple and effective. Cosine annealing with warm restarts (SGDR) can find better minima. Common practice: reduce LR when validation loss plateaus.
hints: Drop LR by 10× when loss plateaus

minigame.title: Valley Descender
minigame.description: Navigate through a 3D loss landscape to find the global minimum. Control your learning rate and momentum to escape local minima and saddle points.
instructions: You are a hiker in fog—you can only feel the slope (gradient) under your feet
Adjust learning rate: too small = slow, too large = fall off cliff
Enable momentum to build speed in consistent directions
Reach the valley floor (minimum loss) as fast as possible!
Avoid getting trapped in local minima or saddle points

codeExample.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ==================== Gradient Descent Variants ====================

def gradient_descent(f, df, x0, lr=0.1, epochs=100):
    """
    Vanilla gradient descent
    f: function to minimize
    df: derivative of f
    x0: initial point
    """
    x = x0
    history = [x]
    
    for _ in range(epochs):
        grad = df(x)
        x = x - lr * grad
        history.append(x)
    
    return np.array(history)

def sgd(f, df, x0, lr=0.1, epochs=100, noise_std=0.1):
    """Stochastic gradient descent with simulated noise"""
    x = x0
    history = [x]
    
    for _ in range(epochs):
        # Add noise to simulate stochasticity
        noisy_grad = df(x) + np.random.normal(0, noise_std)
        x = x - lr * noisy_grad
        history.append(x)
    
    return np.array(history)

def momentum_gd(f, df, x0, lr=0.1, gamma=0.9, epochs=100):
    """Gradient descent with momentum"""
    x = x0
    v = 0
    history = [x]
    
    for _ in range(epochs):
        grad = df(x)
        v = gamma * v + lr * grad
        x = x - v
        history.append(x)
    
    return np.array(history)

def nesterov_gd(f, df, x0, lr=0.1, gamma=0.9, epochs=100):
    """Nesterov accelerated gradient"""
    x = x0
    v = 0
    history = [x]
    
    for _ in range(epochs):
        # Look ahead
        lookahead = x - gamma * v
        grad = df(lookahead)
        v = gamma * v + lr * grad
        x = x - v
        history.append(x)
    
    return np.array(history)

def adam(f, df, x0, lr=0.1, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8, epochs=100):
    """Adam optimizer"""
    x = x0
    m = 0  # first moment
    v = 0  # second moment
    history = [x]
    
    for t in range(1, epochs + 1):
        grad = df(x)
        
        # Update biased moments
        m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * grad
        v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * (grad ** 2)
        
        # Bias correction
        m_hat = m / (1 - beta1 ** t)
        v_hat = v / (1 - beta2 ** t)
        
        # Update
        x = x - lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps)
        history.append(x)
    
    return np.array(history)

# ==================== Learning Rate Schedules ====================

def step_decay(initial_lr, epoch, drop_rate=0.5, epochs_drop=10):
    """Step decay: drop LR every epochs_drop epochs"""
    return initial_lr * (drop_rate ** (epoch // epochs_drop))

def exponential_decay(initial_lr, epoch, k=0.1):
    """Exponential decay"""
    return initial_lr * np.exp(-k * epoch)

def cosine_annealing(initial_lr, epoch, max_epochs, min_lr=0):
    """Cosine annealing learning rate"""
    return min_lr + 0.5 * (initial_lr - min_lr) * (1 + np.cos(np.pi * epoch / max_epochs))

def warmup_schedule(epoch, warmup_epochs, base_lr, target_lr):
    """Linear warmup"""
    if epoch < warmup_epochs:
        return base_lr + (target_lr - base_lr) * epoch / warmup_epochs
    return target_lr

# ==================== Test Functions ====================

def rosenbrock(x, y, a=1, b=100):
    """Rosenbrock function - classic optimization test"""
    return (a - x)**2 + b * (y - x**2)**2

def rosenbrock_grad(xy, a=1, b=100):
    x, y = xy
    dx = -2*(a - x) - 4*b*x*(y - x**2)
    dy = 2*b*(y - x**2)
    return np.array([dx, dy])

def rastrigin(x, A=10):
    """Rastrigin function - many local minima"""
    n = len(x)
    return A * n + np.sum(x**2 - A * np.cos(2 * np.pi * x))

# ==================== Visualization ====================

def visualize_convergence():
    """Compare different optimizers on a simple quadratic"""
    f = lambda x: x**2
    df = lambda x: 2*x
    
    x0 = 5.0
    lr = 0.1
    epochs = 50

    # Run optimizers
    hist_gd = gradient_descent(f, df, x0, lr, epochs)
    hist_momentum = momentum_gd(f, df, x0, lr, gamma=0.9, epochs=epochs)
    hist_nesterov = nesterov_gd(f, df, x0, lr, gamma=0.9, epochs=epochs)
    
    # Plot
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
    
    # Trajectory
    axes[0].plot(hist_gd, 'b-o', label='GD', markersize=4)
    axes[0].plot(hist_momentum, 'r-s', label='Momentum', markersize=4)
    axes[0].plot(hist_nesterov, 'g-^', label='Nesterov', markersize=4)
    axes[0].axhline(y=0, color='k', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
    axes[0].set_xlabel('Iteration')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('x value')
    axes[0].set_title('Convergence Trajectory')
    axes[0].legend()
    axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    
    # Loss over time
    losses_gd = [f(x) for x in hist_gd]
    losses_momentum = [f(x) for x in hist_momentum]
    losses_nesterov = [f(x) for x in hist_nesterov]
    
    axes[1].semilogy(losses_gd, 'b-o', label='GD', markersize=4)
    axes[1].semilogy(losses_momentum, 'r-s', label='Momentum', markersize=4)
    axes[1].semilogy(losses_nesterov, 'g-^', label='Nesterov', markersize=4)
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Iteration')
    axes[1].set_ylabel('Loss (log scale)')
    axes[1].set_title('Loss Convergence')
    axes[1].legend()
    axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def visualize_lr_schedules():
    """Plot different learning rate schedules"""
    epochs = np.arange(100)
    initial_lr = 0.1
    
    schedules = {
        'Constant': [initial_lr] * 100,
        'Step Decay': [step_decay(initial_lr, e) for e in epochs],
        'Exponential': [exponential_decay(initial_lr, e) for e in epochs],
        'Cosine Annealing': [cosine_annealing(initial_lr, e, 100) for e in epochs]
    }
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    for name, lrs in schedules.items():
        plt.plot(epochs, lrs, label=name, linewidth=2)
    
    plt.xlabel('Epoch')
    plt.ylabel('Learning Rate')
    plt.title('Learning Rate Schedules')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

# Run visualizations
if __name__ == "__main__":
    visualize_convergence()
    visualize_lr_schedules()
    
    print("\n=== Gradient Descent Demo ===")
    print("Optimizing f(x) = x² from x₀ = 5")
    
    f = lambda x: x**2
    df = lambda x: 2*x
    
    result = gradient_descent(f, df, x0=5.0, lr=0.1, epochs=50)
    print(f"Final x: {result[-1]:.6f}")
    print(f"Final loss: {f(result[-1]):.6f}")
    
    print("\nWith momentum (faster convergence):")
    result_m = momentum_gd(f, df, x0=5.0, lr=0.1, gamma=0.9, epochs=50)
    print(f"Final x: {result_m[-1]:.6f}")
    print(f"Final loss: {f(result_m[-1]):.6f}")
